mcqs.question: Why does the recommended design keep the read path (queries) separate from the write path (record())?
options: Because the write path needs authentication and the read path doesn't
So query needs — like adding an index — can evolve independently without ever touching the append-only write logic
Because a single audit log can only be written to by one process
Because reads and writes must always run on different physical servers for compliance reasons
mcqs.explanation: Separating reads from writes means the append-only writer stays simple and untouched while the read side adds indexes or search capability freely. Auth isn't the reason for the split, one-writer isn't a real constraint here, and there's no physical-separation rule at play.

mcqs.question: What's the most reliable way to guarantee an audit event isn't lost when the business write and the audit write hit two different systems?
options: Retry the audit write a fixed number of times and log an error if it still fails
Make the audit write fire-and-forget so it never blocks the business transaction
Use an outbox pattern — write the event to a local table in the same transaction as the business change, then reliably publish it from there
Skip auditing for any operation that touches more than one system
mcqs.explanation: An outbox write lands in the same local transaction as the business change, so it can't be silently dropped even if the downstream publish step fails and retries later. A fixed retry can still exhaust and fail silently, and fire-and-forget offers no durability guarantee at all.

mcqs.question: How do you let compliance efficiently answer "show every change to entity X" without scanning the entire audit log?
options: Store the log in reverse chronological order so recent entries are found faster
Shard the log randomly across multiple files
Compress older log entries to reduce the amount of data scanned
Add a secondary index keyed by the target entity's ID, updated alongside each write
mcqs.explanation: A secondary index on the target ID turns "every change to X" into an indexed lookup instead of a full scan, while the append-only property of the primary log stays intact. Reordering, random sharding, or compression don't address the actual access pattern being asked about.

mcqs.question: What's wrong with logging the entire before/after object graph on every audit event, "to be thorough"?
options: It bloats storage and risks capturing sensitive fields like passwords or PII that shouldn't be in an audit log at all
It makes the AuditEvent mutable, which breaks the immutability guarantee
It prevents the log from being append-only
It's actually the correct approach and has no real downside
mcqs.explanation: A full object dump grows storage fast and can capture sensitive data an audit log shouldn't hold, turning a compliance tool into a liability — allow-listed fields are the fix. It has nothing to do with mutability or append-only-ness, and it's a common real mistake, not a correct approach.
